papers.title: Illness Experiences and Supportive Care Needs of Patients With Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: A Qualitative Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: AIMS: To synthesise the holistic illness experiences and supportive care needs of patients with early-onset colorectal cancer across the entire disease trajectory. BACKGROUND: The incidence of early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC), defined as colorectal cancer diagnosed in individuals younger than 50 years, has been steadily increasing. Patients are often diagnosed during critical periods of intimate relationship formation, family building and career development, when financial stability is also being established. This timing can create substantial challenges across multiple domains of quality of life. However, no previous qualitative review has systematically synthesised the illness experiences and supportive care needs of patients with EOCRC. DESIGN: A qualitative systematic review using JBI meta-aggregation and reported in accordance with the PRISMA and ENTREQ guidelines. METHODS: Qualitative studies were included if they explored the illness experiences and supportive care needs of patients with EOCRC. Two reviewers independently conducted study screening and data extraction. DATA SOURCES: We searched PubMed, Embase (Ovid), Web of Science, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, ProQuest, CNKI, WanFang, VIP and Google Scholar. The databases were searched from inception to 28 January 2026. RESULTS: This review included 17 studies. A total of 168 extracted findings were aggregated into 13 categories and four synthesised findings. The four synthesised findings concerned prediagnostic healthcare-seeking difficulties, multidimensional effects of disease and treatment, a lack of age-appropriate supportive services and positive adaptation. CONCLUSION: Patients with EOCRC have distinct illness experiences and require tailored age-specific supportive services to address their unique needs. papers.title: Grateful for What and Whom? How Gratitude List Content Varies and Is Associated With Affective Responses.
papers.abstract: A gratitude list activity, whereby one recalls and writes down things they are grateful for, is a well-studied intervention known to confer an immediate and even prolonged boost in well-being. However, the specific content people reflect on, and how it relates to affective evaluations and the impact of the intervention, remains underexplored. Using data from a global online study (N = 19,265), we applied natural language processing to examine the content of gratitude lists, identifying 16 thematic clusters, with the most common one focused on social relationships. Next, we examined and found various sociodemographic and psychological differences in people's gratitude list content. Further, mentioning themes related to family or nature was associated with greater increases in positivity following the activity. Overall, our findings highlight individual differences in what people naturally think of during this popular intervention and suggest opportunities for personalized modifications to enhance adherence to and effectiveness of the intervention.

papers.title: AI-Mediated Mental Health Support: The Role of Attachment Orientation and Psychological Distress.
papers.abstract: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.

papers.title: Why population-based longitudinal studies are vital for mental health prevention and policy.
papers.journal: The Australian and New Zealand journal of psychiatry
papers.abstract: There has been an increase in the prevalence of mental health problems in young people worldwide for over a decade. Population-based longitudinal studies can help show why this has occurred and whether it will continue throughout life for the present cohort of young people. This in turn will guide the policy response. We discuss two recent articles published in Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry which highlight the value of longitudinal studies in understanding the causal structure of mental health problems. Australia and New Zealand have a rich tradition of longitudinal studies dating to the 1970s, with some studies now enrolling offspring of the original cohorts. Advances in methods, computing technology and the availability of linked administrative data will make these studies even more valuable in future. The studies will need to evolve to capture shifting environmental factors, such as the digital environment. To get the most value from these studies, there needs to be secure long-term investment by central funding agencies and support for vibrant collaboration networks between the studies.

papers.title: From Hippocrates to Biologics, The Evolving History of Pericarditis: A Review.
papers.abstract: Pericarditis remains a common and clinically relevant cardiovascular condition whose diagnosis and management have evolved substantially over time. Understanding this historical progression provides important context for contemporary practice and emerging therapeutic strategies. Early descriptions, dating back to Hippocrates, framed pericarditis as a clinical observation, with more precise diagnostic characterization emerging in the 19th century through the work of Laennec and later refined by clinicians such as Spodick and Hatle. Initial treatment approaches were largely symptomatic or surgical, including pericardiectomy for advanced constrictive disease. The mid-twentieth century marked a shift toward medical therapy with the introduction of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and corticosteroids, which improved symptom control but were limited by high recurrence rates. The advent of echocardiography transformed pericardial disease evaluation by enabling noninvasive diagnosis, hemodynamic assessment, and safer pericardiocentesis. More recently, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging has further advanced care by allowing detailed tissue characterization and improved risk stratification. Randomized trials established colchicine as a cornerstone therapy for both acute and recurrent pericarditis. A major paradigm shift has occurred with the recognition of autoinflammatory mechanisms underlying recurrent disease and the introduction of targeted interleukin-1 inhibition, including anakinra and rilonacept, particularly for refractory cases. Together, these advances reflect a transition from empirical management toward mechanism-based, personalized care. Ongoing progress in imaging, biomarker integration, and targeted immunomodulation is expected to further refine diagnosis, treatment, and long-term outcomes for patients with pericardial disease.

papers.title: High burden of depressive symptoms among sexual and gender diverse persons in Brazil: The role of discrimination, internalized homonegativity, and race.
papers.abstract: Sexual and gender diverse (SGD) populations have historically faced restricted rights and systematic discrimination for deviating from the established hetero-cis-normative norms. This long-standing marginalization has a profound negative impact on health outcomes, including a heightened risk of developing mental health issues, such as depression. Understanding the health-disease process among SGD populations requires recognizing that discriminatory experiences, such as homophobia and transphobia, are not unidimensional, but operate synergistically with layered forms of discrimination, such as racism. We assessed depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) among SGD persons in Brazil using race as a stratification variable. We also evaluated the role of discrimination and internalized homonegativity on depressive symptoms, while adjusting for covariates. This was a cross-sectional online survey recruiting SGD persons aged 18 years or older, living in Brazil, through dating apps and social media. Overall, 6220 participants were included, 3749 (60.3%) White, 1685 (27.1%) Pardo and 786 (12.6%) Black. Mean scores of depressive symptoms was 8.8 (SD7.1), higher among Black (9.6; SD 7.5) and Pardo (9.3; SD 7.2) than White (8.4; SD7.0) (p < 0.0001). Considering a PHQ-9 cut-off of ≥10 points, more Black and Pardo participants reported depressive symptoms than White participants (38.5%, 38.1%; 32.3%, respectively). In multivariable linear regression models, higher discrimination score and younger age were associated with higher scores of depressive symptoms for all races. Additionally, internalized homonegativity and lower income were associated with higher depressive symptoms scores for Pardo and White, but not for Black participants. papers.title: Foundation model-powered deep learning of endometrial histology for predicting the cumulative live birth of an in vitro fertilization cycle.
papers.abstract: Objective and reproducible assessment of endometrial receptivity is essential for optimizing in vitro fertilization (IVF) success, yet traditional histological dating suffers from observer variability. This study investigated whether deep learning of hematoxylin and eosin histology images could support cumulative live birth prediction in IVF. An end-to-end ResNet-18 was compared with a UNI2-h-based pipeline, using UNI2-h as a frozen feature extractor. Ten-fold cross-validation ensembles were developed from natural-cycle endometrial biopsies and evaluated in an internal held-out cohort with live birth outcomes. Additional phase-based evaluation was performed, which tested the performance in distinguishing LH + 7 versus non-LH + 7 phases. A luminal epithelium (LE)-focused design was also assessed to examine whether concentrating on maternal-embryo interface could improve fertility-oriented learning. The whole-slide ResNet-18 model performed well in internal outcome-based testing but near random in external phase-based testing. In contrast, the UNI2-h model with mean pooling and a multilayer perceptron classifier showed less divergent performance, with ensembled AUROCs of 0.74 ± 0.03 in internal outcome-based evaluation, and 0.90 ± 0.05 in external phase-based testing. Despite a smaller training set, LE-focused models retained comparable performance. In internal outcome-based testing, LE-focused ResNet-18 and UNI2-h models achieved AUROCs of 0.71 ± 0.03 and 0.74 ± 0.09 respectively. External phase-based testing yielded AUROCs of 0.80 ± 0.16 for ResNet-18, and 0.84 ± 0.06 for UNI2-h. Grad-CAM review of LE-focused ResNet-18 models showed attention commonly on LE-alone or mixed with adjacent stroma. papers.title: Swiping between worlds: anticipatory family filtering, face-work and gendered reputation in Vietnamese Generation Z university students' use of dating applications.
papers.abstract: This study examined how Vietnamese Generation Z university students negotiate intimacy, reputation, and family authority in dating applications. Using an interpretivist, social-constructionist design, we interviewed 25 students in five Vietnamese cities and analysed the material through theory-informed reflexive thematic analysis, using face negotiation theory, Goffman's dramaturgy, and affordance theory as sensitising concepts. We constructed five themes: multi-audience face-work and layered concealment; friendship-first framing and the cultivation of tình cảm; gendered reputational risk and women's constrained sexual agency; the cultural appropriation of platform affordances; and anticipatory family filtering, in which participants report screening profiles against anticipated parental approval before any interaction. We propose the Anticipatory Face Management Model of Digitally Mediated Romance as a dataset-grounded account of how these mechanisms combine. The analysis locates family authority at the interface rather than after a relationship has been formed, and situates this finding in the regionally and generationally uneven ways Vietnamese family authority and sexual respectability are lived, rather than as part of a homogeneous 'Confucian culture'.

papers.title: The moderating role of support systems in associations between dating violence and depressive symptoms among Black adolescents.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Black adolescents, particularly those in low-income areas, are disproportionately exposed to dating violence. Given the associations between dating violence victimization and mental health, research must explore factors that may mitigate these effects in adolescence. Therefore, we investigated the potential buffering role of family support and nonparental adult (NPA) support in the relation between dating violence victimization and depressive symptoms among 180 Black adolescents. We also tested gender differences. METHOD: This study utilized data from a larger project conducted in the Southeastern United States. The present study was composed of 180 adolescents (aged 12-17 years) who identified as Black or African American. The sample was 51.1% female. RESULTS: Findings indicated that there were no significant gender differences in associations, so findings are for males and females. Psychological dating violence victimization predicted greater depressive symptoms, while family support predicted lower depressive symptoms. Family support and NPA support were both significant moderators. Among adolescents with low family support, psychological dating violence predicted greater depressive symptoms, but this relation was not significant among adolescents with high family support. Additionally, among adolescents with low NPA support, physical dating violence predicted greater depressive symptoms, but this relation was not significant among adolescents with high NPA support. CONCLUSIONS: Findings build on the limited research on dating violence among Black adolescents, highlighting the role of social support systems in protecting against adverse mental health outcomes. papers.title: At-Home Point-of-Care Urine Tenofovir Testing for Adherence Monitoring: Feasibility and Comparison with Adherence Metrics in Dried Blood Spots.
papers.journal: Journal of acquired immune deficiency syndromes (1999)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Scalable, low-cost strategies for monitoring antiretroviral therapy adherence are increasingly important, particularly in decentralized and telehealth-based care settings. This study assessed both the feasibility and performance of at-home, point-of-care (POC) urine tenofovir (TFV) testing for adherence monitoring, using tenofovir diphosphate (TFV-DP) levels in dried blood spots (DBS) as a pharmacological standard of adherence. SETTING: This study was conducted within the LetSync cohort of people with HIV in primary romantic relationships, primarily Black men who have sex with men, across the U.S. METHODS: Participants self-collected POC urine TFV testing and DBS samples over five timepoints across eight months. Adequate adherence was defined as TFV-DP ≥4 doses/week in DBS. Generalized estimating equation models evaluated associations between urine TFV results and DBS-based adherence, as well as the probability of sample return over time. RESULTS: Among 86 participants and 341 paired samples, detectable urine TFV was strongly associated with adequate adherence in DBS (aRR = 2.86; 95% CI: 1.37-5.99). The urine POC test demonstrated high sensitivity (97%) and positive predictive value (85%), with lower specificity (31%). Across timepoints, urine samples showed higher return rates compared to DBS (aRR = 1.04; 95% CI: 1.01-1.08). Participants with detectable viral load had lower return rates for DBS compared to urine. CONCLUSIONS: At-home POC urine TFV testing is a sensitive and feasible approach for monitoring adherence. Its simplicity and consistently high return rates support its potential as a practical adherence monitoring tool, particularly in settings where VL testing is infrequent or logistically limited.

papers.title: Rechargeable Seawater Battery Coupled to Solar Seawater Desalination With a Mutual Enhancement Effect.
papers.abstract: Rechargeable seawater battery (RSWB) is a promising candidate for low-cost energy storage while solar seawater desalination (SSD) can produce clean water from seawater, yet no attempts have been made to integrate them, preferably with a mutual enhancement effect. In this study, we report an ε-MnO2 material with bifunctions of ion storage for RSWB and photothermal effect for SSD. The integration of RSWB and SSD leads to a mutual enhancement effect, in sharp contrast to traditional integrations. The ε-MnO2 displays a high specific capacity of 265 mAh g-1 for RSWB. When coupled with SSD, the specific capacity obviously increases, and meanwhile the seawater evaporation rate also increases substantially during the charge/discharge process. The mutual enhancement effect is attributed to the temperature increase in cathode caused by the photothermal effect of ε-MnO2 and the weakened hydrogen-bonding interaction arising from the charge/discharge process. This work would provide new perspectives on energy storage and clean water production.

papers.title: What Is the Impact of Coercive Control on Children Exposed to Domestic Violence?
papers.abstract: Moving beyond traditional frameworks focused on physical violence, the article adopts a comprehensive definition of coercive control as encompassing psychological abuse, isolation, stalking, and the systematic denial of autonomy, and argues that its effects on children are distinct and deeply harmful, often persisting long after direct exposure ends. Three key mechanisms of harm are identified: (1) credible threats, which compel children and mothers to constantly modify their behavior to avoid punishment, creating a chronically stressful environment akin to "walking on eggshells"; (2) hypervigilance, a state of continuous environmental scanning that depletes cognitive resources needed for learning and healthy social development; and (3) disruption of developmental milestones, including secure attachment, self-regulation, and social competence. Understudied areas require future research, including children's recovery trajectories after separation from a coercive parent, the use of children as surveillance tools by abusers post-separation, and "litigation abuse" whereby legal systems are used to maintain control and destabilize families. The author concludes that effectively protecting children requires recognizing coercive control as a systematic erosion of autonomy and safety, not merely a series of violent incidents, and calls for research to better inform therapeutic interventions and legal policy.

papers.title: Direct Observation of a Hydrogen-Bonding Assisted Quasi-Reversible Superoxo/Peroxo Interconversion in a Heme Model.
papers.abstract: The activation and reduction of molecular oxygen at transition metal centers are central to both enzymatic catalysis and energy conversion. Here, we report the first direct observation of a hydrogen-bonding-assisted, quasi-reversible superoxo (FeIII─O2˙-)/peroxo (FeIII─O2 2-) redox couple in a heme model complex using conventional cyclic voltammetry. Urea groups installed in the second coordination sphere (SCS) of an iron-porphyrin (ααUrFe) form a hydrogen-bonding network that stabilizes the FeIII─O2˙- intermediate through interaction with a trapped water molecule. Spectroscopic studies and DFT calculations reveal that one-electron reduction of the low-spin end-on FeIII─O2˙- species generates a low-spin end-on FeIII─O2 2- adduct with minimal structural reorganization. These findings provide the first synthetic demonstration of a biologically relevant end-on peroxo species stabilized by hydrogen-bonding "pull effect" in the SCS and highlight the critical role of second-sphere interactions in modulating O2 activation pathways in bioinspired catalysts.

papers.title: Förster Resonance Energy Transfer-Based Selective Detection of Influenza Viruses Using N-Doped Sialic Acid Carbon Dots.
papers.abstract: We report the rational design and synthesis of nitrogen-doped sialic acid-derived carbon dots (SiaMPDA CDs) with excitation-independent green emission and high quantum yield and demonstrate their application as efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) donors for the selective detection of influenza A virus (IAV) subtypes. The surface functionalization of the CDs with sialic acid moieties enables specific molecular recognition of the viral hemagglutinin (HA) protein via multivalent hydrogen-bonding interactions. In combination with Rhodamine B (RhB) as an acceptor, the SiaMPDA-RhB pair exhibits efficient FRET under native conditions. Upon interaction with IAV (H3N2 and H1N1), the FRET system displays anomalous spectral behavior characterized by a simultaneous increase in both donor and acceptor emission intensities without any spectral shift. Mechanistic investigations suggest the formation of a ternary IAV-SiaMPDA-RhB complex, wherein long-range charge transfer coupled with FRET governs the observed fluorescence response. Control experiments with proteins, membrane vesicles, and liposomes confirm that the signal specificity arises from targeted interactions between the sialic acid functionalities of the CDs and the viral surface proteins. The sensing platform enables selective and sensitive detection of IAV subtypes in the picomolar range, comparable to existing carbon dot-based detection systems. These findings establish N-doped sialic acid carbon dots as promising nanoscale probes for virus detection and provide insights into charge-transfer-coupled FRET mechanisms in complex bionano interfaces.

papers.title: Thermally Stable Hydrogel Optical Fibers Enable Soft Plasmonic Interfaces for Wearable and Implantable Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Hydrogel optical fibers (HOFs) offer soft, transparent, and biocompatible fiber platforms for biointegrated photonics, yet their practical use in wearable and implantable sensing is limited by thermally induced dehydration, shrinkage, refractive index drift, and optical loss. Here, we report a thermally stable HOF that couples hydrogen bond reinforcement with water-state regulation to stabilize both the hydrogel matrix and the fiber photonic interface. Polyacrylamide-based hydrogel fibers are fabricated by drawing-spinning, followed by thermal treatment, during which drawing-induced chain orientation, free-water evaporation, and glycerol-mediated hydrogen bonding generate dense hydrogen-bonded nanoclusters and a stable bound water. The resulting fibers exhibit smooth cylindrical morphology, a step-index-like refractive index profile, low optical attenuation of 0.136 ± 0.004 dB/cm, high flexibility, and stable light guiding from -10 to 80 °C. Benefiting from the thermally stable and metallizable hydrogel surface, a nanoscale gold film is integrated onto the fiber to construct a soft HOF surface plasmon resonance interface. The HOFs enable wearable skin temperature warning and implantable in vivo body temperature monitoring in mice. This work establishes a material-interface-device strategy for thermally robust hydrogel fiber photonics and expands HOFs from passive soft waveguides toward active plasmonic sensing platforms for wearable and implantable physiological monitoring.

papers.title: Towards a Molecular Understanding of the Role of Helix 8 in GPCR Trafficking.
papers.abstract: Helix 8 in G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) has recently been linked to receptor internalization (Schmidt et al., 2025, Sci. Adv. 11, eadv1499), but the molecular basis of this relationship remains unclear. Here, we examined a proposed mechanism in which helix 8 functions as a surface-active amphipathic element that promotes membrane binding, senses membrane curvature, and thereby facilitates GPCR trafficking. We analyzed six amphipathic peptides, including helix 8 segments from five GPCRs spanning a broad range of internalization rates, using molecular dynamics simulations and circular dichroism spectroscopy. Secondary structure in a membrane environment showed the strongest relationship with internalization, indicating that helix-forming propensity is a key determinant of trafficking behavior. Membrane binding showed a weaker and non-significant association with internalization. Taken together with the attachment to the helix 7 and putative lipid anchors at palmitoylation sites of common helix 8s, membrane binding was assessed not to be a dominant factor for internalization. Curvature sensing, as modeled here, did not correlate positively with internalization, although all constructs favored positive curvature and curvature-related hydrophobic phase width matched the internalization trend. Together, the results suggest that, while membrane binding and curvature-related properties likely contribute to the process, the ability of helix 8 to form amphipathic helices is the principal factor underlying differential GPCR internalization. These findings support a broader model in which surface-active amphipathic motifs tune membrane protein trafficking by coupling dynamic structural propensities to membrane interactions.

papers.title: Burden, perception of stigma, and gender differences among informal care partners of individuals with mild cognitive impairment.
papers.abstract: BackgroundCaring for individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is increasingly recognized as a significant clinical challenge. However, the latent burden, driven by perceived stigma and gender-specific vulnerabilities, remains poorly characterized during these early stages of cognitive decline.ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of care partner strain and affiliate stigma, and to identify independent correlates of psychological distress and protective factors among informal care partners of individuals with MCI.MethodsWe conducted a multicenter, observational, cross-sectional study across 19 memory clinics in Spain. Care partners (n = 196) were evaluated using the Zarit Burden Interview, Affiliate Stigma Scale, and validated instruments assessing resilience, relationship quality, coping strategies, and psychological distress. Multivariate logistic regression models identified independent predictors of burden and stigma.ResultsSignificant care partner strain affected 59.7% of the cohort, while 39.3% perceived themselves as stigmatized. Multivariate analysis revealed that high burden was independently associated with anxiety symptoms (OR = 1.13, p = 0.017) and perceived stigma (OR = 1.07, p = 0.007). High resilience served as the primary determinant protecting the 60.7% of partners who did not report significant stigma (OR = 1.05, p < 0.001). Compared to their male counterparts, female care partners were significantly younger and reported higher levels of burden, anxiety, and stigma.ConclusionsCare partner strain and affiliate stigma are correlated phenomena that emerge long before formal patient dependency. These findings underscore the need for gender-sensitive clinical frameworks and specific interventions that actively strengthen resilience immediately upon MCI diagnosis to mitigate early psychological deterioration.

papers.title: Adaptive fuzzy super-twisting sliding mode control with nonlinear active disturbance rejection for electromechanical stabilizer bars to improve vehicle roll stability.
papers.abstract: Electromechanical stabilizer bars are commonly equipped in luxury vehicles to enhance rollover stability during aggressive steering maneuvers at high speeds. However, most existing studies simplify actuator and vehicle dynamics, while parametric uncertainties, model nonlinearities, and external disturbances are often insufficiently addressed. This paper proposes a robust adaptive control framework for an active anti-roll system with three main contributions. First, a comprehensive coupled dynamic model is established to explicitly capture the interaction between the electromechanical stabilizer-bar actuator and vehicle dynamics. Second, an integrated Super-Twisting Sliding Mode Control and Nonlinear Active Disturbance Rejection Control scheme is developed, in which the nonlinear extended state observer estimates and compensates for lumped disturbances and uncertainties, while the super-twisting mechanism provides robust motor current tracking. Third, an adaptive fuzzy gain-scheduling mechanism adjusts the control gain online according to vehicle operating conditions. The novelty therefore lies in the coordinated integration of coupled actuator-vehicle modeling, disturbance compensation, robust current tracking, and operating-condition-dependent gain adaptation within an electromechanical stabilizer-bar control framework. Numerical simulations demonstrate superior performance to the benchmark controllers in reducing vertical tire-force variations and improving vehicle dynamics. Under a J-turn maneuver at 100 km/h, the maximum motor-current tracking error is limited to 0.11 A, with an overshoot of 3.59% and a settling time of 0.17 s. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and potential of the proposed framework for automotive active control systems.

papers.title: Attachment Styles, Resilience, and Parenting Attitudes Among Adolescents Exposed to Interparental Intimate Partner Violence.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the relationship among the resilience levels, attachment styles, and the parenting attitudes of adolescents who did and did not witness interparental intimate partner violence (IPV). The study included adolescents and their mothers who presented to the Child-Adolescent Psychiatry clinics. The case and control group consisted of adolescents who had and had not witnessed interparental IPV, respectively. Data were collected using the K-SADS-PL-DSM-5-T, a sociodemographic data form, the Child and Youth Resilience Measure, the Three-Dimensional Attachment Style Scale, and the Parental Attitude Research Instrument. Resilience levels were significantly lower in the case group. In the control group, secure attachment style was observed more frequently, while avoidant and anxious-ambivalent attachment styles were more prevalent in the case group. Resilience was positively related to secure attachment and negatively related to avoidant and anxious-ambivalent attachment in both groups. Regarding parenting attitudes, the case group scored higher on the Rejection of the Housewife Role and Marital Discord subscales. In conclusion, the adjustment of children exposed to interparental IPV depends not only on traumatic experiences but also on resilience, attachment styles, and parental attitudes. Therefore, intervention programs should integrate trauma-focused approaches with strategies that strengthen parent-child relationships and foster protective factors enhancing resilience. This study examined how witnessing violence between parents affects adolescents’ ability to cope with stress, their emotional bonds with others, and the parenting approaches they experience at home. We compared adolescents who had witnessed violence between their parents with those who had not. papers.title: A sex-positive approach to sexual rehabilitation after SCI: exploring women's sexual experiences using participatory action research.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To explore the sexual experiences of women living with spinal cord injury (SCI) and collaborate with key partners to identify needs of women with SCI related to sexuality interventions. METHODS: Participatory action research (PAR) was employed which involved the researcher collaborating with an advisory team consisting of women with SCI and clinicians. A sample of 15 Canadian women with different levels/severities of SCI participated in semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis was employed to analyze interview data. RESULTS: Three main themes were identified: relationship with the self, changes in the body, and intimacy with partners. Participants noted that sexuality was a critical aspect of their relationship with themselves and connected it to self-confidence. They also discussed the importance of self-exploration. Changes in the body resulted in feelings of grief and vulnerability. Finally, the women discussed intimacy with partners emphasizing critical experiences including incorporating sex toys/assistive devices, exploring kink and fetish, orgasm, fertility, and how sexuality and intimacy enhanced their quality of life. CONCLUSION: This study advances the field of rehabilitation as it is the first study to include women with SCI as collaborators in sexual rehabilitation research and the first to explore women's sexuality after SCI from a sex-positive lens. Women with Spinal Cord Injury experience grief, vulnerability, and a reduced sense of confidence as a result of their injuries.Sexual health is a priority for women with Spinal Cord Injury and is intimately connected with their mental, psychological, and emotional well-being.Healthcare professionals are encouraged to develop educational resources to address the sexual health needs of women with Spinal Cord Injury focusing on topics such as self-confidence, sex toys/assistive devices, normalizing and navigating and grief post injury.

papers.title: Between Institutional Fragmentation and Victim Resilience: A Critical Analysis of Support Mechanisms for Women Victims of Intimate Partner Violence in Morocco.
papers.abstract: This article examines institutional responses to intimate partner violence (IPV) in the Fes-Meknes region of Morocco across the health, judicial, and police sectors. Using a qualitative sociological design, it draws on semi-structured interviews with 44 women victims of IPV and 41 professionals. Data were analyzed through an inductive thematic approach informed by Braun and Clarke's framework. The findings reveal major gaps in institutional support, including unequal access to services, procedural burdens, limited emotional support, weak follow-up, and fragmented coordination. Overall, the study highlights the gap between formal protection mechanisms and their implementation, and calls for more integrated, victim-centered institutional responses.

papers.title: Post-Traumatic Growth and Depreciation Among Women Exposed to Intimate Partner Violence: The Predictive Role of Core Beliefs and Resilience.
papers.abstract: Traumatic experiences can lead to negative changes in an individual's evaluations of themselves, others, and the world by disrupting their belief systems. The purpose of this study is to examine post-traumatic depreciation (PTD) and post-traumatic growth (PTG) in women exposed to physical violence by an intimate partner, as well as the psychological factors potentially associated with these variables. The research was conducted with 72 female participants aged 19 to 63 reached through purposeful sampling. Findings indicated that psychological resilience has a strong protective effect on PTD, whereas the disruption of core beliefs is a risk factor that significantly predicts PTD. Contrary to expectations, no significant relationship was found between the disruption of core beliefs or psychological resilience and PTG. This result suggests that in chronic and interpersonal traumas, the shattering of the belief system does not spontaneously lead to PTG; instead, it may contribute to PTD when the disruption remains unrepaired. These findings indicate that in clinical interventions for survivors of violence, targeting PTG alone may not be sufficient; interventions aimed at strengthening psychological resilience and repairing disrupted core beliefs play a critical role in preventing PTD.

papers.title: Men's Experiences With Image-Based Sexual Abuse in the United States: Victimization Contexts, Emotional Experiences, and Perceived Vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Image-based sexual abuse (IBSA) is a growing form of technology-facilitated sexual violence, with increasing prevalence across the globe and significant psychological and social consequences. This study explores the unique experiences of United States men victim-survivors of IBSA using a transcendental phenomenological approach to examine how they interpret the interpersonal contexts surrounding their victimization, the forms of abuse they experience, their emotional responses, and the factors they perceive as shaping their vulnerability. Findings highlight the role of intimate partner dynamics in facilitating abuse, with victimization commonly occurring following relational conflict. Participants also described blackmail and retaliatory dissemination as the primary forms of abuse and reported profound emotional consequences following their victimization. Socioeconomic circumstances and social identities also emerged as perceived vulnerability factors. This study underscores the importance of addressing the gendered nature of IBSA, where men (stereotypically framed as perpetrators) are increasingly recognized as victims of this form of abuse. The results call for a reexamination of societal norms around sexual violence and the legal system's response to IBSA, emphasizing the need for more inclusive support structures and policies that account for the unique experiences of male victims.

papers.title: Intimate Partner Violence Among Postpartum Women in Low-Income Developing Rural Areas: A Cross-Sectional Study in China.
papers.abstract: Intimate partner violence is a global issue with severe impacts on women's health, especially during pregnancy and postpartum. Living conditions for mothers in rural areas are characterized by transportation isolation, low literacy levels, lower economic status, limited access to healthcare, and social norms that condone violence. These specific cultural, social, and economic factors have contributed to the worsening of intimate partner violence in rural areas. However, the current situation of intimate partner violence among women during pregnancy and the postpartum in low-income rural areas of China remains insufficiently explored. To examine the prevalence and factors influencing intimate partner violence among women during pregnancy and postpartum in low-income rural areas of China. A cross-sectional study was conducted using a set of general questionnaires covering demographic, obstetric/pediatric, and psychosocial characteristics, together with two validated instruments, namely the Abuse Assessment Screen for intimate partner violence and the Social Support Rating Scale for social support. Among 467 women, 82 (17.6%) experienced intimate partner violence during pregnancy and postpartum, including 74 (15.8%) emotional, 15 (3.2%) physical, and 20 (4.3%) sexual violence cases. Additionally, 2.1% of the participants experienced all three types of violence. Receiving care from partners or their families and social support were protective factors, while the number of pregnancies, partner alcohol abuse during pregnancy, negative life events, and supportive attitudes toward intimate partner violence were risk factors. The findings indicate that targeted interventions and educational efforts should focus on altering sociocultural perceptions and behavioral patterns, particularly the attitudes of partners and family members. Future research should thoroughly investigate the long-term effects of various forms of support (e.g., emotional, financial) and the support system

papers.title: Assessing coercive control in intimate partner relationships: psychometric validation and clinical thresholds of a French version of the Coercive Control Screening Scale (CCSS-F).
papers.abstract: Background: Coercive control is increasingly conceptualized as a chronic relational pattern of domination that may function as a mechanism of traumatization over time. Sustained exposure to intimidation, isolation, surveillance, and credible threat has been linked to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), complex PTSD (CPTSD), and depressive symptomatology. Despite its relevance for trauma-informed assessment, no validated French-language instrument exists, and no empirically derived cutoff score has been established for the original Coercive Control Screening Scale (CCSS).Objective: This study aimed to translate and validate a French version of the CCSS (CCSS-F) and to establish the first empirically derived cutoff score to support clinically meaningful screening of coercive control exposure.Method: Following forward-backward translation and expert panel review, 304 French-speaking women (18-70 years) were recruited, including 225 community participants and 79 women receiving hospital-based psychiatric care for documented intimate partner violence and trauma-related difficulties. Participants completed the CCSS-F and validated measures of battering (WEB), relationship abuse, post-traumatic stress symptoms, depression, relationship dissatisfaction, perceived social support, and social desirability. Factor structure (EFA/CFA), reliability (α, ω), construct validity, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were conducted.Results: The CCSS-F demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α and ω > .90) and a stable unidimensional structure. Strong associations were observed with battering and relationship abuse (ρ > .80), and moderate associations with PTSD and depressive symptoms, supporting convergent validity. papers.title: Heightened intimate partner violence and sexual risk taking among male military sexual assault survivors.
papers.journal: Psychological trauma : theory, research, practice and policy
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Military samples are a priority for sexual health interventions. Military sexual assault (MSA) exposure may increase risk for sexual risk taking, particularly among male survivors. Previous research indicates that intimate partner violence (IPV) is more strongly associated with negative behavioral health outcomes in male MSA survivors than their female counterparts, suggesting that there may be a similar association between IPV and sexual risk taking. The present study hypothesized that sex would significantly moderate a positive relationship between overall IPV exposure and sexual risk taking, such that it would be stronger for male survivors. IPV subdomains of psychological aggression, sexual coercion, and physical assault were also examined. METHOD: Using data from a survey of MSA survivors collected in 2021 (N = 346; 50.9% male), sexual risk taking was regressed on overall IPV (or the IPV domains), sex, and their interaction. RESULTS: The interaction between overall IPV and sex was statistically significant, B = 0.19 (SE = .07), p = .006, such that the overall IPV was positively associated with sexual risk taking for both sexes, but the effect was stronger for male survivors, B = 0.36 (SE = .05), p < .001, relative to female survivors, B = 0.17 (SE = .05), p = .001. Associations of psychological aggression, sexual coercion, and physical assault with sexual risk taking were significantly moderated by sex such that they were only significant for male survivors. CONCLUSIONS: Findings highlight unique outcomes military male survivors face and point to a need for including these survivors in future investigations of MSA and IPV. papers.title: Changes in parent-grandparent relationship quality and links with parents' distress throughout the transition to parenthood.
papers.journal: Journal of family psychology : JFP : journal of the Division of Family Psychology of the American Psychological Association (Division 43)
papers.abstract: The transition to parenthood marks an important turning point for parent-grandparent dyads, as parents' needs for grandparental support increase and grounds for both emotional closeness and conflict arise. Guided by a life-course perspective, this study investigated changes in parent-perceived emotional closeness and conflict between parents and grandparents throughout the transition to parenthood, as well as linkages with parental symptoms of anxiety and depression. Longitudinal biannual questionnaire data of 385 Dutch first-time parents (37.9% male) covering several years before and after the birth of a first child were analyzed using piecewise latent growth models. The results indicated an average decrease in emotional closeness and no change in conflict posttransition, which differed significantly from the stability in emotional closeness and decline in conflict found pretransition. On average, mothers and fathers did not differ in their perceptions of parent-grandparent relationships, and the associations between relationship quality and symptoms of distress were mostly evident at intercept. After the transition, parents who reported less decrease in closeness with grandparents tended to experience a stronger decrease in depressive symptoms, but not anxiety symptoms. These findings were interpreted in the context of parental expectations, gender norms, individual variability, and methodological limitations. Future studies should examine the temporal ordering of the changing dynamics between parents and grandparents during this key life transition.
